articles.title: Sleep vs. shutdown: When to use these modes on your mini PC - Engadget
articles.text:
Sleep vs. shutdown: When to use these modes on your mini PC
You'll probably use sleep more, but shutdown has its benefits.
While mini PCs don't offer the performance or expansion capabilities of a full desktop, they make for excellent everyday computers. Their small footprint also makes them ideal for a home server or a media center. In many cases, they use relatively efficient hardware compared to traditional PCs.
In fact, you'll find that many mini PCs actually contain laptop-grade hardware under the hood. The only differences between a mini PC and a laptop are that mini PCs don't contain a battery and have beefier cooling hardware that tends to result in better sustained performance. But unlike a laptop where you can simply close its lid and put it away, a mini PC asks you to choose between sleep, shutdown and sometimes hibernation options when you're done using it. So when should you use the sleep and shutdown modes? In general, sleep is better for short periods, while shutdown allows you to unplug the mini PC.
Sleep vs. shutdown modes
If you're simply stepping away from your mini PC for a few minutes, putting it to sleep is the best choice as it allows you to resume within seconds. Even with modern SSDs, you'll have to wait a couple of minutes before reaching the desktop if you shut it down completely.
But what about when you're walking away for extended periods of time? I would still personally favor sleep mode, as it allows you to keep your programs open for later. The downside is that the mini PC still draws some power in sleep mode, even if it's considerably less than when the computer is up and running.
If you don't care about running programs, though, a full shutdown allows you to unplug the mini PC altogether. This can be valuable if you live in a region with high electricity rates, although it's not worth worrying over in most cases. Mini PCs in sleep mode consume about one to four watts of power, which will barely register on most power bills. A full shut down, which closes open applications, can be useful to give your computer a fresh start from time to time, though.
If you want the best of both worlds, consider Windows' hibernation feature instead. When you use hibernation, your PC saves the current state of any open programs to your disk before completely powering down. When you turn the PC back on, it restores your previous session including any open applications and documents. Hibernation is similar to a full shutdown, which means you can unplug the computer from the wall. The only downside is that booting a hibernated PC takes longer than resuming from sleep.
You don't have to worry about wearing out your mini PC's internal components when it's in sleep mode either. The small amount of power running through them won't cause any major damage, unless you experience frequent brownouts or similar electrical anomalies. Capacitors and other electronic components were much more sensitive to breaking down with constant power running through them in prior decades, but that's no longer the case these days.
Your mini PC can remain powered on 24/7 too
I have two mini PCs tucked away in a closet and drawer. One runs a self-hosted smart home server and the other serves media from my personal collection. In either case, I need them to be ready at a moment's notice — nobody in my family wants to wait several minutes for a movie to load, for example. And even when I'm away from home, I can stream media from the mini PC over the internet.
The good news is that mini PCs consume very little power, especially when you aren't running a performance-hungry application. Computer power draw generally increases with CPU load (and GPU load, if your mini PC has one). At idle, modern computers tend to sip power, and mini PCs are particularly good at keeping power consumption low.
Depending on the exact processor, memory and storage components in your mini PC, you can expect it to draw between 10W and 15W from the wall at idle. This number can go up if you add SSDs and especially hard drives to your mini PC, but we are still only talking about the difference of a few watts.
For some context, if your mini PC averages about 10 watts of power draw when idle, you can expect it to consume just over 87 kilowatt hours (kWh) annually. How much you will pay for that consumption depends upon your local rates, but assuming the average residential US electricity rate of $0.18 per kWh, you'll end up paying around $16 a year to keep your mini PC powered 24/7. Of course, the true cost will be higher depending on how frequently you use the mini PC for demanding tasks.

Nỗ lực ngoại giao giữa Mỹ và Iran giúp giá dầu hạ nhiệt, giảm lo ngại lạm phát. Đồng USD suy yếu cũng hỗ trợ giá vàng. Kim loại quý đạt đỉnh tuần tại 4.148 USD/ounce.

Đến thứ Tư, giá vàng chính thức đánh mất mốc 4.000 USD/ounce. Những phát biểu cứng rắn của các quan chức Fed tiếp tục củng cố kỳ vọng thắt chặt tiền tệ.
Đà giảm mạnh hơn trong phiên thứ Năm khi lợi suất trái phiếu kho bạc Mỹ tiến sát 5%, đồng USD tiếp tục tăng giá. Vàng chạm đáy tuần tại 3.852 USD/ounce. Lực mua bắt đáy xuất hiện khi giá xuống mức thấp nhất kể từ tháng 10/2025.

Ông Chandler cảnh báo thị trường chưa hình thành vùng đáy. Mục tiêu giảm tiếp theo của vàng có thể thấp hơn khoảng 100 USD. Nếu giá xuyên thủng vùng 3.750 USD/ounce, kim loại quý có thể lùi về 3.500 USD/ounce.

articles.title: Nvidia pressed Taiwan over indicted manager
articles.text:
Nvidia raised concerns with Taiwanese political officials after prosecutors charged one of its managers in a chip smuggling case, Bloomberg reported. It cited people familiar with the matter.
Nvidia’s representatives said they disagreed with the charges against the manager, surnamed Chang, the people said. They also said he should not be under investigation. The officials replied that they had no role in the case.
Chang was detained in July and indicted in August on forgery and breach of trust charges. Prosecutors in Keelung call him the core figure in a network that sent 74 servers with Nvidia chips to China. Another 56 were seized.
Prosecutors say Chang helped win Nvidia’s approval to sell 130 servers to a buyer without the data centre space for them. They also say he hid that the payment came from a Chinese entity.
Nvidia told Bloomberg it had looked into the case.
“We investigated this matter thoroughly, as is our standard practice, and found no indication that our employee knew of the alleged diversion effort by employees at other companies,” the company said.
It added that it engaged with authorities, as any company would, to provide information they asked for and to look after its employee.
Chen Po-wen, a spokesman for the Keelung prosecutors, told Bloomberg the office was unaware of Nvidia’s contacts with the government. It is unclear which request for information Nvidia meant.
Nvidia also asked TSMC, its main manufacturer, for advice, Bloomberg said. TSMC declined to get involved. Nvidia has no government relations director in Taiwan and only recently advertised the role.
The approach echoes Washington. There, Nvidia’s general counsel called a Commerce official about the Megaspeed probe, which was later paused. Megaspeed denies wrongdoing.
Its founder, Alice Huang, is suspected by US officials of spying for China, which Beijing denies. Jensen Huang resigned as chief executive last week after admitting an affair with her. The two are not related.
Chang faces up to five years in prison. Bloomberg could not reach him for comment.

Now through the end of today, November 15th, the 55-inch model is 50 percent off, dropping it to an all-time low of $699.99 ($700 off) at Best Buy. LG’s budget-friendly B6E OLED TV is up to 50 percent off this weekend
The excellent OLED offers great contrast and plenty of gamer-ready features at a fraction of the cost.
Although it’s not as bright as LG’s pricier C6, the B6E still delivers the excellent contrast and deep blacks OLEDs are often praised for. It’s nearly identical to the standard B6, except it comes with a simpler remote that lacks the motion controls and voice features found on LG’s Magic Remote. It may lack some of the more advanced features found on LG’s more premium OLED TVs, but at 50 percent off, the B6 is a great option if you want the benefits of OLED without spending a fortune.

articles.title: New Species of Giant Fungus Discovered in China Grows up to 20 Inches Tall
articles.text:
Sometimes new species evade detection because they’re tiny and thus easy to miss—not this giant fungus. Shaped like a hand reaching out of the ground, this new species of fungus was discovered deep in the forest in China’s Yunnan Province. A research team from the Kunming Institute of Botany, part of the Chinese Academy of Sciences, reported it as a new species they named Dianjunus rex.
The name comes from the region’s ancient Dian Kingdom and the Chinese pronunciation of the word fungus. D. rex is a type of Ascomycete, the largest phylum of fungi, with over 64,000 known species, and among them, this new fungus produces the largest masses of mushroom recorded. Unlike what we typically think of as a “mushroom,” Ascomycetes don’t form caps and stems but produce structures called fruiting bodies, which release spores to reproduce. And growing up to 20 inches and weighing nearly 5 pounds, D. rex’s are huge.
Within the Ascomycetes, the giant fungus constitutes an entirely new biological family (the broader classification of genus and species), meaning that it has no close relatives—at least that we know of. While 6,000 fungal species have been documented in Yunnan, mycologists believe the province known for its biological diversity could easily harbor 100,000
“The discovery illustrates how much fungus biodiversity remains to be discovered in East Asian forests,” Indunil C. Senanayake, an associate professor at the Kunming Institute of Botany and the lead author of the paper, said in a press release.
Senanayake and his research team conducted surveys in the Nanban tropical rainforest, where they came across large, whitish fruiting bodies growing in the soil near the roots of dying trees. They documented and collected fungi growing in a wide variety of shapes like cylinders, spindles, and cupped palms. The fruiting bodies appeared to develop finger-like branches upon maturity. They found that the above-ground portions are covered with white, powdery fibers that turn dark yellow as the fungi mature, while the portions buried in the soil are black and smooth.
The fruiting bodies dried rapidly when the scientists took samples back to the lab. They found that the interiors were dense and sponge-like, appearing white or yellow with no strong odor or taste. (Don’t try this experiment at home.)
Analyzing the DNA of these fungi, the researchers reconstructed a “molecular clock,” which revealed that D. rex diverged from other species approximately 65 million years ago. This is the end of the Cretaceous period, immediately following the mass extinction that is believed to have wiped out three-quarters of all plant and animal species, including the dinosaurs. That means D. rex and T. rex never met, but this era was likely a boon for fungi. Large quantities of dead plant material became available following the die-off, which could have provided new ecological opportunities for fungi and other organisms that decompose such matter.
Genomic analyses, however, indicated that D. rex doesn’t have nearly as many decomposition-related genes as the scientists expected. Compared to some of its closest relatives that also feast on plant matter, the huge fungus has only about half the usual number of decomposition-related genes.
Senanayake has a theory about this. Although they have so far only found the fruiting bodies around dying plants, the fungus may be leading a “double life”—living inside healthy trees and then feeding on dead plant material when the hosts die. That could perhaps explain how D. rex is able to store enough energy to build the massive fruiting bodies.
This is just a theory for now, but the giant fungi undoubtedly do need a surplus of energy to grow so large. Senanayake hypothesizes that the benefit of these large fruiting bodies is that they tower higher than the surrounding plants and fallen leaves, which could be advantageous for wind-mediated spore dispersal in a dense forest. “However, such a large structure requires substantial energy investment, suggesting that this strategy likely evolved only where the ecological benefits outweighed the costs.”
This story was originally published in WIRED Japan and has been translated from Japanese.

articles.title: Open-ear vs. in-ear earbuds: Which is actually better for your ears? - Engadget
articles.text:
Open-ear vs. in-ear earbuds: Which is actually better for your ears?
Each type of earbud has its perks and pitfalls.
With the very different designs of open-ear and in-ear earbuds, you might be wondering if one kind is better for your ears than the other. Since in-ear buds go in your ears, similar to earplugs, they offer a tight seal and direct sound into your ear canal. This can provide some level of pressure, especially if you wear them for hours. They are also more prone to getting dirty from secretions like earwax. By contrast, open-ear buds sit atop your ears so there's minimal contact. They wrap or clip around the top or bottom of the lobe, some even with bands that position behind the neck. Bone conduction models rest on your temple and transmit audio to your ears via vibrations.
It's not just about which option is better for your ears, as there's also a trade-off in sound quality and noise cancellation versus comfort. When it comes down to it, while there are fewer potential issues linked to open-ear buds, you also won't get as good a sound experience as you would with in-ears since the audio isn't as focused. Plus, ambient noise will still be audible. With proper wear and care, though, in-ears are perfectly fine for limited use.
The upsides and downsides of in-ears
As noted, in-ear buds completely seal your ear canal, which isolates outside sound and focuses audio directly into your ear. This offers an advantage in sound quality and noise cancellation. You get better bass and richer, more immersive sound with music, and crisp, clear audio for phone calls. They can also block ambient sounds, like the hum of an airplane or people milling about. This occurs through both passive and active noise cancellation: they physically plug your ears (passive), and many models use microphones and algorithms to further cancel out noise (active).
But there are downsides. Since they plug the ear, there's some pressure, which can lead to ear fatigue over time. They can also cause irritation for some, especially for those who suffer from sensitive skin or conditions like eczema. Wax and moisture build-up can also be an issue. Users who tend to turn the volume up too high risk damaging their hearing, especially if they exceed safe levels for long periods of time. This isn't necessarily an issue with open-ear headphones since they aren't plugging your ears and filtering sound right into the eardrum.
Because of the pressure and isolation, you won't want to wear in-ears for hours upon hours. That said, if you limit usage, keep them clean, and maintain safe volume levels, in-ear buds can be perfectly fine. They are not necessarily "worse" for your ears. But they present risks you don't have to worry about with open ears.
Why open ears might be better for your ears
Sound quality is rarely as good with open-ear models since they don't seal the ear. Since sound isn't directed into your ear canal, you may need to crank the volume, resulting in sound leakage so others around you can hear the audio.
With open-ear buds, you don't typically get noise cancellation, though the Shokz OpenFits Pros are an exception with proprietary noise reduction. It works well, but doesn't rival in-ears. With open-ears, you remain more aware of your surroundings, though many in-ears have transparency and awareness modes to use as needed as well, so you're not completely oblivious to the world.
Furthermore, while some people find in-ears don't fit right or are uncomfortable, some open-ears may not sit perfectly either. That's especially the case for clip-style buds on larger lobes. But most open-ear models are more secure than you may think, even during rigorous workouts. And they are usually more comfortable since nothing is plugging your ears.
The main upside is that they're more hygienic and thus better for you in the long term unless you're extra diligent about cleaning your in-ear buds. However, the concessions with sound quality and noise cancellation are important to consider if you go this route. But overall, open-ear buds pose little to no risk to your ears or hearing.
Given this, for occasional, focused listening, especially in noisy environments, in-ears are the way to go. For everyday casual listening, long wear periods where sound quality and noise cancellation aren't the priority and sweaty outdoor fitness activities like running where you want to remain aware of your surroundings, open-ear buds are the better option.

articles.title: Data centres demand power guarantees from Big Tech
articles.text:
Data centre developer Applied Digital has asked tenants including Oracle and Meta for billions of dollars in guarantees before signing leases, Bloomberg reported. The money secures power for the sites, it said, citing a person familiar with the matter.
Applied Digital is also asking chipmakers Nvidia and AMD for guarantees, the person said. These are set case by case. They usually cover the cost of grid links.
Credit ratings now decide who gets space. Applied Digital has capped how much it leases to junk-rated neoclouds such as CoreWeave, Bloomberg said. That avoids the extra utility demands tied to weaker tenants.
“Applied Digital prefers to do business with investment-grade tenants, with a preferred mix of 70% investment-grade to 30% non investment-grade,” chief executive Wes Cummins said in a statement to Bloomberg.
CoreWeave told Bloomberg its partnership with Applied Digital is strong. Meta had no comment, and Oracle declined to comment.
Utilities used to fund grid upgrades and recover the cost through rates. Now they want the biggest users to carry that cost if a project collapses. The pressure is rising after the midterms, where Democrats who campaigned on power bills won key races.
Oracle has already felt it. Wisconsin regulators require large customers rated below A- to post collateral. Oracle said its Lighthouse campus could need more than $7bn. It sued the regulator in June, then dropped the case in August.
Indiana’s Nipsco took another route. Its parent NiSource set up a separate unit, GenCo, so Amazon, Google and Microsoft pay for the power plants that serve them.
“We did not want customers to wear the liability,” NiSource executive Michael Luhrs told Bloomberg.
Nipsco has signed 5 gigawatts of GenCo deals, according to Bloomberg. NiSource puts the savings for existing customers at about $1.75bn.
The guarantees land as AI debt piles up. Hyperscalers are expected to issue $300bn to $320bn of debt this year, Barclays estimates.

articles.title: The Sony Aibo was a robot revolution dressed like a dog
articles.text:
In the 1990s, Sony was absolutely convinced that we were on the precipice of a robot takeover. Pretty soon, the company decided, we’d all be living among countless humanoid robots. Some would be our coworkers; others would be our friends; and at least one would be our pet. And “pet” was exactly what Sony was going for when it created the Aibo. It was supposed to be part of the family.
The Sony Aibo was a robot revolution dressed like a dog
On Version History: How a robot dog became a family member, but not exactly a huge hit.
On this episode of Version History, we go back in time and tell the story of the Aibo. David Pierce is joined by The Verge’s Victoria Song and Jennifer Pattison Tuohy, and together they discuss the origins of this remarkable robot dog, and its impressive success and longevity. They also try to figure out why Aibo had such an effect on its owners, what Sony got right (and wrong) about robots, and whether the idea of a robo-pet will ever be a global phenomenon.
This is the first episode of the sixth season of Version History. We’re back! This season is all about pets: gadgets that are pets, gadgets for your pets, and one gadget called pet. We’ll be in your feeds for the next six weeks — if you want to be sure not to miss anything, there are a few ways to subscribe:
If you’re a Verge subscriber, you can also get access to Version History (and all our other podcasts) with no ads. All you have to do is visit your account settings.

articles.title: Italy orders Meta to pay $887M for not obtaining specific consent over user photos - Engadget
articles.text:
Italy orders Meta to pay $887M for not obtaining specific consent over user photos
Meta is reportedly planning to appeal the fine.
The Italian Data Protection Authority (IDPA) has hit Meta with one of its highest fines to date. According to the Italian data regulatory body, Meta failed to specifically disclose that it had access to user photos, videos and the related metadata for those using the Facebook app on Android devices. The IDPA fined Meta Platforms Ireland Limited 805 million euros, or approximately $887 million, which represents 0.47 percent of the company's global revenue.
For users, the "Camera roll sharing suggestions" recommends users which photos or videos to post on Facebook from their phone's photo library. The Italian authority said that access to this photo gallery is granted from a single permission request that applies to the entire app, despite the multiple functions it covers. The IDPA argued that this method allows Meta broad ongoing access without "obtaining specific consent and without properly informing" its users.
Beyond the lack of specific consent, the IDPA argued that the feature shouldn't be on by default and that Meta should make clear that its users are authorizing media gallery access for post suggestions. The Italian data watchdog said it launched the investigation in July 2025, following a complaint from the Bolzano Consumer Protection Centre.
Meta has 60 days to get "separate and specific" user consent for this feature while explaining what it's for and how to disable it. The tech giant also has to switch the feature to off by default, even for those who have already agreed to the permission request. We reached out to Meta for comment and will update the story when we hear back. Meta is also currently dealing with a ruling from a New Mexico judge requiring the social media giant to pay $25 billion in penalties as a result of the personal data harvesting scandal with Cambridge Analytica.

articles.title: Japan's economy unexpectedly contracts in third-quarter as elevated energy costs bite
articles.text:
Japan's economy unexpectedly contracted in the third quarter, shrinking at an annualized 0.1% compared to the previous quarter, as elevated energy prices impacted consumption and net exports.
A Reuters poll of economists had estimated the economy to grow at 0.3% in the three months to September, while GDP had expanded at 1.4% in the previous quarter.
Japan's exports beat expectations for two of the three months in the quarter, but net exports weighed on the economy due to higher costs of energy imports, cutting 0.6 percentage point from the country's growth.
The GDP data could complicate Japan's policy normalization path, though there's still a 75.6% chance of the Bank of Japan raising rates by 25 basis points in December, according to LSEG.
Marcel Thieliant, head of Asia Pacific at Capital Economics, also expects the BOJ to go ahead with the rate hike. "It looks increasingly likely that the Bank will have to tighten policy more aggressively than we've been anticipating as inflation is about to surge."
The BOJ had declared that its 2% underlying inflation target had been met for the first time in 13 years at its meeting last month. Core inflation in September also hit its highest level this year at 2.1%, overshooting analysts' expectations. 
On an year-on-year basis Japan's economy grew 1.1%, its strongest growth since the second quarter of 2025. Theliant noted that this was owed to a lower base in the third quarter of 2025.
Following the data release, the Nikkei 225 fell 0.62%, while the yield on the benchmark 10-year Japanese Government Bonds was at 2.885%. The yen weakened marginally against the dollar, trading at 159.76.

articles.title: I've owned this stock for a decade. AI slowdown fears gave me an opportunity to buy more
articles.text: We've owned Caterpillar for more than a decade, and last week we added to our position at $581 in the Enhanced Dividend Income Portfolio. The stock's recent performance is an important part of the story. Caterpillar had already been under pressure before the election, and its shares fell another 11% over the two days following. Election-related concerns about the pace of data-center development added pressure to companies exposed to the AI infrastructure buildout. Our purchase price was approximately 46% below Caterpillar's June 30 record high. We take those concerns seriously. Delays in data-center projects can affect demand and the timing of deliveries. But we believe the selloff gave us an opportunity to add to a diversified business we have followed and owned for a long time. Key Points AI needs power and physical infrastructure. The bull case is broader than just data centers. Dividend growth signals stability. Why I'm buying AI needs power and physical infrastructure The 101-year-old Caterpillar is still relevant in the AI age. First, it's well-known equipment helps build data centers, but its engines, generators and turbines help power them. Third-quarter results demonstrate the demand with revenue rising 17% to $20.7 billion, and adjusted earnings per share increasing approximately 45% to $7.20. Power-generation sales grew 30%. Caterpillar also generated $3.8 billion in third-quarter free cash flow from its Machinery, Power and Energy businesses. The bull case is broader than just data centers Caterpillar's construction, mining and energy segments all grew as well last quarter. These businesses will always be cyclical, but the Caterpillar investment case doesn't depend on a single datacenter project. Total return Caterpillar raised its dividend by 8% this year, the 32nd straight year it it has done so. While the yield is still only a tad over 1%, management's commitment to the payout shows this is a more dependable company than recent volatility indicates. We are attracted to the combination of dividend growth, cash generation and potential long-term total return. Why now? The shares are more than 40% off their record high reached in June. CAT YTD mountain Caterpillar, YTD While its current price-earnings ratio of 23.5 is neither cheap nor expensive, it is well below its 10-year average of 28. Bottom line We believe Caterpillar's recent decline created an opportunity to add to an established business with exposure to the infrastructure needed to power AI and the broader economy. articles.title: Stock futures tick higher as traders brace for Nvidia earnings, Anthropic IPO this week: Live updates
articles.text:
Stock futures ticked higher on Sunday night following a volatile week on Wall Street, as traders await a highly anticipated earnings report from Nvidia and a potentially record-setting public market debut.
Nasdaq-100 futures gained 0.6%, while S&P 500 futures advanced 0.3%. Dow Jones Industrial Average futures traded 71 points higher, or 0.1%.
In Asia, markets opened lower Monday, with Japan's Nikkei 225 leading losses after third-quarter GDP unexpectedly shrank. The index slipped 0.63%, while the broad-based Topix was down 0.24%. South Korea Kospi was down 0.1%, while the small-cap Kosdaq was 0.56% lower. Australia's S&P/ASX 200 declined 0.12% as well.
Nvidia is set to report results after the bell on Tuesday. While analysts expect the chipmaker to post nearly 100% year-over-year earnings and revenue growth, investors will be more focused on how the company will move forward after Jensen Huang's exit as CEO.
Huang last week resigned from his post after reports of multiple extramarital affairs, including one with an alleged Chinese spy. Nvidia shares dropped 13%, marking their biggest weekly slide since April 2025.
"The main task at hand for interim CEO Colette Kress [is to] restore order and give the Street confidence in the Nvidia story going forward," wrote Dan Ives, analyst at Yorkville Ives. "This starts with earnings and the conference call this week on Tuesday after the bell…we still expect guidance and a typical conference call around robust business metrics with demand metrics that have clearly accelerated since last quarter."
Another key catalyst is Anthropic's initial public offering. The AI giant is eyeing a roughly $1.4 trillion valuation, with shares expected to be priced between $70 and $78.
Wall Street is coming off a winning week despite Nvidia's tumble.
The Dow, S&P 500 and Nasdaq posted their biggest weekly gains since August, rising more than 2% each.

articles.title: What I know and respect about Colette Kress, the person now leading Nvidia
articles.text: Many of you Club members have had the good fortune of making hundreds of thousands of dollars — or even millions of dollars — from investments in the now-bedraggled Nvidia because of my long-standing support of the company and its stock. I may have met you at our Club meeting last October , when now-former CEO Jensen Huang was our featured guest. Or at one of the numerous Fosforo bottle signings at Total Wine, as lots of people bring their brokerage statements to those. Or at a ballgame where you fought through a crowd to tell me that you hit it out of the park with the biggest win I can ever recall. I am blown away with how many millions of dollars so many of you have made, and how kind you are when I meet you. Please, keep coming up to me when you see me so we can rejoice together — but only if some of it has been taken off the table . You know how I am about diversification. At last year's Club meeting, Huang was incredibly gracious in saying that he wanted to thank me for being loyal and sticking by him through thick and thin — and we forget there were plenty of thins. I was embarrassed because I did nothing to make this the greatest semiconductor company ever, and then the most valuable company on earth for a time. I said that, but Huang didn't want to hear it. He was too effusive in praising me; he always was, doubling down when I renamed my mutt Nvidia in 2017 . If I had any regret at that Club luncheon, or at any other time that people have told me they became wealthy with one stock, it's that I didn't tell you the other person who should have been praised, who played an incredibly important role in the wealth-creating process: Colette Kress, the company's longtime CFO and now interim CEO. She assumed the additional role Thursday, when Huang resigned amid a broadening affair scandal. At this very moment, the only thing many people know about Kress comes from a Wall Street Journal story published Thursday night , which carried this headline: "Before His Ouster, Jensen Huang Belittled the Executive Replacing Him." In the story, The Journal reported, based on a person familiar with the matter, that Huang called Kress "a deer in the headlights" and a "reporting" CFO during a meeting this summer. These are two incredibly damning labels, the first implying that she is in over her head, and the second implying that she's a bean counter. I hope these loathsome epithets are just the product of the heat of the battle, the things that get said at the giant staff meetings that Huang has periodically. I am not in a slag Huang mode, but in light of what happened to him, you could argue that the real "deer in the headlights" was Huang. If he wanted a wartime CFO to try to make some of these deals across the artificial intelligence ecosystem look better, he picked the wrong person. Kress is by the book, even as she presided over a slew of investments and financial guarantees for companies such as OpenAI. You can find all this ecosystem support in Nvidia's financial statements, with the company disclosing roughly $530 billion in off-balance-sheet commitments and guarantees at the end of last quarter. Many of these deals look like vendor financing, something we hated during the dot-com era, and yet have accepted at this time because of the outstanding value of the firm's graphics processing units, or GPUs. Essentially, these vicious comments, as reported by The Journal, made it sound like Kress is a joke. But, for those of us who've interacted with Kress extensively, the joke was on Huang. I believe she was trying to exert discipline and restraint in a way that ruffled his feathers. NVDA 5Y mountain Nvidia's five-year stock performance. One of the myriad duties that Kress had as finance chief was to speak to large institutions and the press. For years, I spoke to her after every conference call, usually at 6:30 p.m. ET. Clockwork. There were many moments when I was baffled by something, or didn't understand it because I am not a technologist. I am a generalist. I have to spend as much time learning potato chips as semiconductor chips. I have to go through so many reports just to handle the Lightning Round on "Mad Money." Kress has always been willing to walk me through everything, even at times when I felt like the proverbial five-year-old asking the question. What you may not know is how many times her explanation kept me in the stock when others were busy upgrading or downgrading, doing the things that kept people from turning thousands of dollars into millions. She did it not by strapping me to the mast, or giving me blithe reassurances that I should trust her. She took the time to explain. It mattered. One time, for example, Nvidia missed the quarter because of an issue involving bitcoin mining. Nvidia's GPUs were being used by cryptocurrency miners in record numbers until a sudden plummet in price led to a huge drop in mining and therefore sales of its chips. Kress explained it to me and admitted that she had gotten the numbers wrong because she didn't have insight into that mysterious crypto channel, so she didn't know about an inventory build caused by a collapse in prices. She apologized. She didn't need to do so. An explanation would have been enough, but in her patient way, she had to let me know that she would do better next time. And she did. She never missed again. That element of humility is very rare in these kinds of calls. Because of it, and her powerful bearing, I told people to stick with Nvidia when so many others were running from it. There were several instances where I questioned the valuation. She would patiently work me through why a certain valuation might be considered appropriate given the future. It always made sense. Again, it's why I reiterated buy to you over and over and over. Huang would help. I would see him at dinners, at conferences, in interviews, and at the annual GTC conference — I can't believe I won't see him any more — and most of the time we talked about innovation and the future. Very little substantive was said about our families, although he did meet my wife, Lisa, one night for dinner, sat next to her and was terrific to her. She liked him very much. But it was Kress who did the explaining in such a way that I felt emboldened to say "own it, don't trade it" and we only took some off when we thought we were being pigs and elevated uncertainty called for some prudence. Kress also provided a conduit to Huang. I had been suggesting to Kress that Nvidia adopt a much more aggressive buyback, and I was quite strident. She took it to Huang and came back to me with some of the company's parameters that differed with mine. I could tell Huang was far more lukewarm about it, even as I kept saying that the best CFO ever, the now-retired Luca Maestri of Apple, shrank the iPhone maker's share count by roughly 40% during his decade-plus tenure. In doing so, he had a real hand in the company's expanding price-to-earnings valuation and success for shareholders. I dropped it as a cause because I did not want to alienate Kress. And I was also critical of Huang through Kress for not taking some profits on some of the big wins he had on his investments — in particular, Intel. As part of a technology collaboration announced in September 2025, Nvidia bought $5 billion worth of Intel stock at $23.28 per share. The stock would go on to catch fire and trade well over $100 this year. What did he need to prove? Intel had been saved and his investment became a huge hit. Why not take some, if not all, off the table and use it to buy back his own stock? If not that, he could deploy the profits into one of his many deals to get the AI ecosystem off the ground. It was clear Kress believed my logic was cogent, but Huang disagreed again. He was firm in his insistence that the ecosystem needed his support, which often turned into vendor financing. Not my favorite use of capital, but not for me to blast given its success to date. No matter. I was heard because of Kress. Kress is now going to run the company until a full-time CEO is picked. This thoughtful, razor-sharp person will do a terrific job because she listens, she learns, she explains, and she is not afraid to speak her mind. The coda? We know Huang reportedly derided Kress as a deer in the headlights. What we don't know is what she was saying to him that he called her out with such vicious opprobrium. Was it the billions he wanted to give companies that perhaps didn't deserve it? Was it the commitment to invest $100 billion in OpenAI in September 2025 that sewed up nothing because OpenAI announced a huge deal with Nvidia's chief rival, Advanced Micro Devices , a couple of weeks later? Was it to question an initiative being led by Huang's son-in-law ? Somehow, in retrospect, I think if we knew the context, you would know why I think the world of Colette Kress because I can assure you that she had the institution's interests first. Sadly, I no longer can say that about the man himself. Kress has the backing of the board as the right person for this job. Additionally, I now understand that many people, including myself, thought Huang was running the company, because, in many ways, Kress was back at the ranch while Jensen cavorted and promoted all around the globe. He was everywhere, driving the world to understand what the future would look like. He showed me this AI future a decade ago, and he nailed it right on time. One of the reasons I am more confident than most about Nvidia — although I must retire its "own it, don't trade it" designation — is that Nvidia has a multiyear technology roadmap that every engineer and leader is executing on. The business team, led by Kress, is in charge of execution and it has been flawless. That's what makes me so confident, even as I worry about institutional shareholders who believe that, like Steve Jobs, Huang was the company and he took it with him. Now just a word about Huang himself. I think the people who say he was unfairly dismissed are looking only at the stock price and the success of the company, and not the ethics or national security issues that must be considered. I am not overlooking that his return would be best for shareholders, or even the company, in the short term. But it is a public company. There is a board. It's their job to preserve the institution and no one, including Huang, is above that principle. (Jim Cramer's Charitable Trust is long NVDA. See here for a full list of the stocks.) articles.title: Trump breaks silence about FAA nationwide ground stop, blames Biden administration
articles.text:
President Donald Trump on Sunday made his first public comments about Friday's nationwide ground stop by the Federal Aviation Administration, blaming the Biden administration for making an "old and broken" air traffic control system worse. Trump also urged Congress to approve more funding to modernize the system.
The ground stop lasted more than four hours Friday, disrupted flights nationwide, contributed to thousands of cancellations and delays, and affected hundreds of thousands of passengers.
"The Biden Administration was an FAA disaster," Trump wrote on his social media platform. "Big money spent unwisely, making an old and broken system worse than when they began."
The president added that his administration has "the knowledge and plan for the Flight Control Systems," but said that "we need Congress to give the money, FAST!"
Congress approved $12.5 billion for the FAA last year as part of a major tax and spending package. Transportation Secretary Sean Duffy has said that the aging air traffic control system will need more funding for a broader overhaul.
The FAA said its equipment became unstable after a high volume of data flooded its network. The agency said contractor work at one site may be related and that the underlying cause remains under investigation.
Nationwide FAA ground stops are rare. Before the Nov. 2026 shutdown, the last two were after the Sept. 11 attacks and a brief FAA computer outage in January 2023.

articles.title: Bessent calls for ‘dramatic shakeup’ at Nvidia, urges outside CEO
articles.text:
Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent on Sunday called for a "dramatic shakeup" at Nvidia after CEO Jensen Huang's resignation, questioning whether the chipmaker pursued illicit sales of its advanced artificial intelligence chips to boost earnings.
Bessent said Nvidia's board should look outside the company for its next chief executive and suggested other executives should face scrutiny over the chip giant's compliance with U.S. export controls.
"I want to keep coming back to what was the culture at Nvidia, and were they pressing these seemingly illicit sales to goose their revenues and their earnings?" Bessent said in an interview on Fox News.
The remarks come amid a growing feud between Bessent and Commerce Secretary Howard Lutnick over the suspected diversion of advanced AI chips to China, even as the Treasury secretary continues to defend President Donald Trump's handling of the matter.
Both Bessent and Lutnick are expected to accompany Trump to China this week, Semafor reported Sunday, putting the two Cabinet secretaries alongside the president as he prepares to meet with Chinese President Xi Jinping and Russian President Vladimir Putin on the sidelines of the APEC summit.
A White House official told Reuters on Thursday that the president maintains "complete confidence" in Lutnick, despite mounting scrutiny of the secretary’s handling of the Nvidia matter.
Huang resigned Thursday following revelations about his relationship with Alice Huang, a former executive at Singapore-based Megaspeed, whom U.S. intelligence officials suspect of spying for China. Megaspeed is suspected of diverting Nvidia chips to China in violation of U.S. export controls.
Nvidia named Chief Financial Officer Colette Kress interim CEO.
Bessent suggested Sunday that Nvidia's problems extended well beyond Huang.
"If this were a bank and they hadn't complied like this, the OCC would be in there right now, and a lot of the executives would be removed," Bessent said, referring to the Office of the Comptroller of the Currency.
Bessent also questioned Nvidia's financial disclosures, pointing to a surge in reported Singapore revenue as its China sales fell.
Nvidia stopped separately reporting Singapore revenue in November 2025, saying a new methodology based on customers' headquarters rather than billing addresses better reflected the geographic distribution of its sales.
Bessent's remarks came two days after he told CNBC's "Squawk Box" that several federal agencies had supported adding Megaspeed to the government's export blacklist for months.
"But Commerce has the pen," Bessent said.
The public rebuke followed reporting by Axios that Bessent confronted Lutnick in the White House Situation Room over Commerce's failure to act against Megaspeed. Commerce denied that the confrontation took place.
Lutnick is also facing scrutiny over his family's financial ties to Nvidia. CNBC reported Friday that Cantor Fitzgerald, the Wall Street firm formerly run by Lutnick and now led by his sons, has helped arrange billions of dollars in financing for Nvidia's business partners.
Cantor said Nvidia share holdings fell nearly 50% over six months as national security concerns surrounding Huang escalated. The positions were associated with client swap transactions, not proprietary investments, the investment bank said.
There is no evidence Lutnick shared sensitive information with his sons or that Cantor traded on such information.
Bessent on Sunday said Trump had drawn a firm line against sales of chips more advanced than Nvidia's H200 to China. Trump himself authorized H200 sales to approved Chinese customers in December —following months of lobbying by Huang — in an arrangement under which the U.S. government would receive a 25% cut.
Bessent's latest criticism comes two days before Nvidia is scheduled to report its first quarterly earnings since Huang's departure.

articles.title: Entrepreneur may be the best 'everyday job' of the AI future, says VC investor Alexa von Tobel
articles.text:
Many people dream of being their own boss, but are afraid to take the leap since building a new business can require significant time and money, and a specialized set of skills. But artificial intelligence is lowering these barriers, creating new opportunities for aspiring entrepreneurs. And even for those who have not considered the entrepreneurial route before, it should be on their minds in the AI era, says serial founder Alexa von Tobel.
"Entrepreneurship will be the everyday job of the future," she said during the latest episode of CNBC's Changemakers podcast. "I think every person here in America will be empowered to be entrepreneurial because of AI."
Von Tobel took a leap of faith when she walked into the admissions office at Harvard Business School and formally took a leave of absence to launch a startup during the 2008 financial crisis. "Everyone thought it was a terrible idea, and I've swum against the grain myself," she said.
That idea turned into financial planning company LearnVest, which she ended up selling to Northwestern Mutual in 2015. Von Tobel went on to co-found venture capital firm Inspired Capital with former U.S. Secretary of Commerce Penny Pritzker in 2019.
Von Tobel's interest in financial literacy and financial success was born of her own early life experiences. After her father died when she was 14, her mother, a nurse practitioner, was left to navigate the family's financial situation on her own. The experience made von Tobel realize how little financial education many people receive. Financial security is an issue which AI may make even more critical, but she is optimistic about the future of entrepreneurship, believing more people will be able to turn their skills, knowledge and expertise into businesses of their own.
"Anybody with any skill set can turn it into a business because of AI," she said.
She also suggested entrepreneurship could become a fallback for people between jobs, giving them a way to earn money while they retrain or look for their next role.
Recent data highlights increased interest in starting a business, and, in particular a solo business. Liya Palagashvili, a labor economist and director of the Labor Policy Project at George Mason University's Mercatus Center, recently told CNBC that her preliminary research on new business formation shows it is rising among owners who do not expect to become employer firms — in other words, they have no current expectation of hiring employees. In industries highly exposed to AI, business applications without early signs of hiring rose 26.8% from the first quarter of 2024 through the first quarter of 2026.
"Entrepreneurship feels like a very big commitment," von Tobel said. "I actually think it's going to become a low-stakes commitment."
Von Tobel stressed that while AI will be a business-enabler, the founder always has to have the final say. "At the end of the day, it's still our judgment, my judgment, making that final call," she said.
Von Tobel's Inspired Capital is focused on startups that could become very large businesses — worth $10 billion or more. But among the firms she has invested in, there is a link to the world of "everyday" business owners — including solo businesses, gig work and the ability to turn almost any skill into a source of income.
She pointed to ShopMy, a company backed by Inspired Capital, which created a platform that enables creators to earn income by sharing product recommendations and collecting commissions on purchases. The platform also uses AI-powered matching algorithms to analyze creator profiles, audience engagement and brand objectives, helping brands identify creators that best align with their goals.
"ShopMy is really entrepreneurship skills and tools for creators," von Tobel said.
She believes platforms like it could give people more ways to build income around what they already know, with more flexibility for people balancing work with family or caregiving.
OpenAI CEO Sam Altman said on David Senra's "Founders" podcast that "we are about to see the greatest boom in people starting smaller businesses that we have ever seen."
Von Tobel says her experience raising money for LearnVest included an important lesson about pitching your business idea to investors, and taking money from the right ones. She realized some of the investors advising her had never built a company. "All the people I'm taking capital from have never built anything," she recalled. That gap helped shape the idea for Inspired Capital. "I knew the capital I wanted, and I didn't see it anywhere," she said. "I kept thinking, 'One day, I'm going to come back and build that."
She also says that when pitching ideas to potential investors, having a clear and compelling view of the long-term win is critical. Von Tobel meets with as many as 100 companies a week, but may ultimately invest in less than eight firms a year. She looks for founders with a distinct view of their industry and what it could become. "They will have thought deeply about what the world should look like in five years, 10 years, 20 years," she said.
Follow and listen to "CNBC Changemakers: Women Leading in the Age of AI" wherever you get your podcasts.

articles.title: 3 big things we're watching in the stock market in the week ahead
articles.text: Another Nvidia earnings week is upon us, but this one will be unlike any other. The chipmaker at the heart of the artificial intelligence boom reports quarterly results Tuesday evening, marking Nvidia's first earnings report in its 27-year history as a public company without Jensen Huang as CEO. Huang resigned last week amid a widening scandal over alleged affairs. Ever since Nvidia stunned Wall Street with its guidance in May 2023 , the company's earnings reports and conference calls have been can't-miss events. They've offered a crucial checkup on the health of the AI spending surge and a chance to hear from the visionary executive whose company enabled much of the innovation and created trillions of dollars of shareholder value. Tuesday night will still be can't-miss, but for different reasons. Gone will be Huang's big-picture commentary and visions for the future. Instead, interim CEO and longtime CFO Colette Kress will have to make the case for one of the most consequential technology companies of our time. Nvidia will share the spotlight this week with what could be one of the most consequential tech companies in the decades to come, Anthropic. The Claude chatbot creator is set to go public on the Nasdaq on Thursday in a historic IPO that will test investors' appetite for AI stocks. On top of all this, we will hear from three more companies in our portfolio: Home Depot , TJX Companies and Palo Alto Networks . One saving grace: The economic calendar is fairly light, with retail sales, industrial production, and minutes from the Fed's October meeting as the main releases. Let's take a closer look at what to expect: 1. Nvidia earnings: There is so much that could be said to preview Tuesday night's report. Will it help stabilize Nvidia shares, or unfold in a way that catalyzes further selling? Maybe it will go well, but scandal-related developments away from the earnings report itself will control the stock. The range of outcomes is vast, which underscores why Jim Cramer recommended last week that investors who've built up big gains in Nvidia over the years book some profits . We want to focus on some of the biggest questions for the earnings call, though this is far from an exhaustive list. Will Nvidia stand by its 70% revenue growth forecast for fiscal 2028, which starts in February? What is the risk associated with potential tightening of U.S. export controls on chip shipments to China (or the broader Asia Pacific region)? Are there any updates on the monster stock buyback program, in size or implementation strategy How is Kress planning to approach Nvidia's financial support to other companies in the AI ecosystem going forward? Finally, should we expect any changes to Nvidia's product roadmap and pace of innovation? Nvidia shares are limping into Tuesday's report. So far in November, the stock is down 20%, on pace for its worst monthly performance since ChatGPT sparked the AI boom in late 2022. Here's what analysts are expecting for the quarter, according to LSEG: Revenue: $109.08 billion EPS: $2.47 Conference call starts at 5 p.m. ET NVDA YTD mountain Nvidia's year-to-date stock performance. 2. Other Club earnings: Home Depot kicks off our week with its report before Tuesday's opening bell. The once-struggling stock has mounted a strong rebound since early October, coinciding with the recent peak in the 10-year Treasury yield above 5.3%. With Home Depot relying on housing market activity to drive business, its stock is highly sensitive to the interest-rate backdrop. It got hurt as rates rose amid the war in Iran. Now the reverse is playing out. Will Home Depot's third-quarter results be strong enough to solidify the bounce, or could it open the door to profit-taking? Are they seeing any green shoots in transactions? Key metrics to watch include same-store sales and gross margins, which last quarter benefited from tariff refunds that offset rising incremental costs. Some refund offset is expected again in the third quarter, but what does the fourth quarter look like for magins? We'll also pay close attention to the performance of its professional distribution arm, SRS , and Home Depot's Pro business more broadly. Finally, we await an update on the health of CEO Ted Decker, who took a leave of absence in August. Revenue: $42.79 billion EPS: $3.84 Conference call starts at 9 a.m. ET HD YTD mountain Home Depot's year-to-date stock performance. Off-price retailer TJX Companies reports Wednesday morning. We need to see its Marmaxx division — home to Marshalls and TJ Maxx stores in the U.S. — get back on track after a major letdown in the July quarter. CEO Ernie Herrman attributed the same-store sales shortfall to the company not having "the right goods in the right stores at the right time." He said TJX was addressing self-inflicted issues and that sales trends had already begun to improve by the time of the Aug. 19 earnings call. So, in the results Wednesday, we need evidence that these better sales trends carried through the October quarter and are reflected in its holiday quarter guidance. While we've long viewed TJX as best-of-breed in the discount retail landscape, Ross Stores is a more credible competitor under the leadership of ex-Boot Barn chief Jim Conroy. If TJX is able to right the ship, that will support management's contention that the hiccup was internal rather than the result of intensifying competition. To protect against a letdown, we trimmed TJX on Friday. "There will be big repercussions if they don't make a comeback," Jim said Friday. Revenue: $15.84 billion EPS: $1.34 Conference call starts at 11 a.m. ET TJX YTD mountain TJX Companies' year-to-date stock performance. Palo Alto Networks rounds out the week of earnings Wednesday night. Shares have cooled off after a blistering April-to-October rally, which may help temper expectations ahead of the print. We have little doubt that AI is driving demand for cybersecurity solutions, but the overarching question is how quickly it shows up in the numbers. Last quarter, it did so impressively, as Palo Alto's closely watched next-generation security annual recurring revenue (NGS ARR) grew by a better-than-expected 63% year over year. That also marked a sequential acceleration from the 60% growth rate observed in the April quarter. Where will NGS ARR land this time around? Other metrics to watch include net new platformizations — key to Palo Alto's strategy of customers consolidating their cyber spending — and total remaining performance obligations (RPO), a measure of contracted business not yet converted into revenue. Aside from the actual business performance, will CEO Nikesh Arora be asked about his interest in another top job (at Nvidia)? Revenue: $3.31 billion EPS: $0.97 Conference call starts at 4:30 p.m. ET PANW YTD mountain Palo Alto Networks' year-to-date stock performance. 3. Anthropic IPO: The fast-growing startup is expected to price its IPO on Wednesday night and begin trading the following day. According to its latest securities filing, the company is looking to raise up to $64.4 billion, alongside a $26 billion private placement from a who's-who of tech giants. The stakes for the broader AI trade are massive. Jim summed it up nicely on "Mad Money" last week : "Anthropic is important because it is one of just a few companies at the end of the food chain for all of the AI data center investments that we've seen, so it is one of the few companies that, ultimately, needs to make money from all of this investment spending. If it can't do that, or if it cannot convince enough investors that it will do so, then it's tough to justify all of the AI investments that are being made today." For now, the good news is that interest in the deal is high, with Bloomberg News reporting that it's six times oversubscribed. It doesn't end there. How the stock trades in the days and weeks that follow will be important, especially for other AI-related companies seeking to go public. A final thought: Jim has long warned that new equity supply coming into the market could lead to selling in other names, as investors raise money to buy the hot new issue. It's a dynamic to monitor across our portfolio and the broader market.
